title: the API key in the build environment is not an API key
symptom: Planning to call the Anthropic SDK directly, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY was present in the environment and looked usable.
wrong_hypothesis: "The key is already set, so the LLM layer can assume a working client and we can skip the offline path."
cause: The key is aero_live_…, a Claude Code harness credential scoped to the agent runtime, not an sk-ant-… Anthropic API key. A raw SDK call would have 401'd, and it would have 401'd for the first time somewhere deep in Phase 3 with half the pipeline already written against the assumption.
fix: The LLM layer is an interface with pluggable backends from the start (src/deduction_desk/llm/), so no call site ever names a provider. This turned out to matter more than expected — see Entry 1, where the whole project moved to local inference without a single call-site change.

title: the target machine has no GPU, and no Ollama either
symptom: The project was re-scoped to run entirely on local inference via Ollama, with zero API spend. Before choosing a model, checked what was actually installed.
wrong_hypothesis: "Ollama is presumably installed, and model selection is a matter of picking the best of the 8B–14B candidates." The task brief itself framed it as "8B-class, then a 12–14B if hardware allows", which invited an assumption about hardware.
cause: Two findings, both material: 1. Ollama is not installed at all — no binary on PATH, no ~/.ollama, nothing listening on 11434. 2. The machine is an i5-13500H with 15.7 GB RAM and Intel Iris Xe integrated graphics (~1 GB VRAM). There is no discrete GPU, so every token is generated on CPU. The second one reframes the model choice. A 14B at Q4_K_M is ~9 GB — it *fits in RAM*, which is the check people usually make, and then runs at roughly 2–3 tokens/second, which puts a full 400-invoice batch well past a single night. "Hardware allows" is a question about throughput, not capacity, and the two give opposite answers here.
fix: Three consequences, all landed before any inference was attempted: - Schemas were designed tighter than the brief asked for. evidence_needed became a 2-item enum list rather than free text, and rationale is capped at 200 characters, on the reasoning that output tokens are the entire cost on CPU. Roughly 40 tokens saved per classification is about ninety minutes off a full batch. - doctor measures tokens/sec on the actual machine and converts it into a wall-clock estimate per task, so the go/no-go on a model is a number rather than a hope. - The candidate list in config/llm.yaml is ordered smallest-first and the 12B is explicitly marked as conditional on the 8B failing the F1 floor *and* the clock allowing it — rather than as the natural upgrade. Still open at time of writing: Ollama is not installed, so the empirical model selection in docs/MODEL_SELECTION.md cannot run yet. The entire LLM layer, its tests, and doctor were built and verified without it — 42 tests green, with the 3 live-model tests skipping cleanly.

title: the invoice distribution made two tax rules unreachable
symptom: Generating the batch failed loudly: could not stage showcase scenario(s): SHOW-CREDIT-HOLD, SHOW-HUMAN-QUEUE. Neither a ₹42,000 scheme claim nor a ₹1.8L damage dispute could be placed on any invoice.
wrong_hypothesis: "The showcase constraints are too strict for a 60-invoice batch; widen to 400 and they will find a home."
cause: They did not find a home at 400 either. Measuring the distribution showed why: The problem was never the showcases. Drawing 1–5 line items at random quantities produced a narrow band with a ₹34 minimum — which is not an invoice, it is a rounding error — and nothing above ₹1.66L. That quietly broke three things that had nothing to do with the demo: 1. TDS u/s 194Q only applies above ₹50L of aggregate purchases. No invoice was anywhere near it, so a whole reason code in the taxonomy could never legitimately occur. 2. human_review_threshold_paise is ₹50,000. With deductions running at 1–10% of a ₹35k invoice, essentially nothing would ever route to a human. 3. No case was large enough to make a credit-hold conversation plausible. The failing showcase was a symptom. The batch was quietly incapable of exercising three of its own policy rules, and every one of those would have reported a confident zero.
fix: Invoice values are now drawn by order size class — small / medium / large / bulk, each with a log-uniform target value — and quantities are solved backwards from the target. The distribution is now heavy-tailed like a real order book: median ₹2.1L, p90 ₹23L, max ₹1.42Cr, 16 invoices above ₹50L. Separately, s.194Q is now gated on a buyer-level aggregate, not per invoice, because that is what the section actually says: below ₹50L of purchases nobody deducts, above it the buyer deducts 0.1% on every subsequent invoice including small ones. Same for the TCS/194Q overlap, which is the whole reason that confusion exists. Worth keeping: the generator failing loudly on an unstageable showcase is what surfaced this. A version that quietly skipped the scenario would have shipped a batch that silently could not test three policy rules.

title: DetachedInstanceError building the generation summary
symptom: generate completed the whole batch, then died on the summary: Instance <DeductionTruth> is not bound to a Session; attribute refresh operation cannot proceed.
wrong_hypothesis: "Something is wrong with how the truth records are constructed." Spent a moment looking at truth.py, which was fine.
cause: SQLAlchemy expires every persisted object on commit. The summary reads the same truth objects it just wrote, *after* session_scope has committed and closed — so each attribute access tried to reload from a dead session. The error surfaces a long way from its cause, and it points at the object rather than at the session.
fix: Session(engine, expire_on_commit=False) in db.py::session_scope. These are plain value objects written once and never concurrently mutated, so there is nothing to go stale; the default is protecting against a hazard this codebase does not have.

title: every classification was paying for two generations
symptom: With the model finally running, the test suite showed WARNING llm repair: task=classify on essentially every call. The pipeline worked, and the answers were right, so nothing was obviously broken.
wrong_hypothesis: "The model occasionally emits malformed JSON; that is what the repair loop is for." Reasonable, and wrong — it was not occasional. A probe repeating one prompt four times measured 1 repair on 4 of 4 calls. It was systematic.
cause: The model returns "confidence": 100, meaning certain, where the schema declares le=1.0. Pydantic rejected it every time. The deeper point is why the schema did not prevent it. Ollama compiles model_json_schema() into a GBNF grammar, and a grammar can constrain structure and type but not value — maximum: 1 and maxLength: 200 are simply not expressible in it. So "structured output" guarantees you will get a JSON object with a float called confidence; it guarantees nothing about that float being in range. The model was free to emit 100, and did, every time. The cost was not correctness — the repair recovered — it was the clock. On a CPU box at 6.3 tokens/second a repair is a second full generation. Every classification was costing twice what it needed to, which on the projected batch is roughly two hours of pure waste.
fix: Two mode="before" field validators on Classification: - confidence above 1 is read as a percentage and divided by 100. - rationale and check are truncated to their own caps rather than rejected. The output tokens are already spent by the time the string can be measured, so rejecting buys nothing; and neither field is decision-relevant — no policy rule reads them. Measured after: repairs 1 → 0 on 4 of 4 calls. doctor now projects 4h58m for the full batch rather than roughly ten hours. Worth keeping: the lesson generalises beyond this bug. Treat a JSON Schema handed to a constrained decoder as a description of *shape*, and put every *value* constraint behind a validator that normalises rather than rejects. A rejection in a local-inference pipeline is not a cheap error path; it is the most expensive thing in the system.

title: "same prompt twice → identical output" is only true warm
symptom: test_same_prompt_twice_is_byte_identical failed in the full suite but passed when run on its own.
wrong_hypothesis: "Test pollution — some earlier test is leaving state behind." Nothing was shared: the test already used two separate empty cache directories precisely so both calls would be live.
cause: The difference was not other tests, it was model residency. In the full suite it was the first call after a cold 4.7 GB load; alone, the model was already resident from keep_alive: 30m. Unloading the model and re-running reproduced the failure immediately. Measured behaviour: | condition | raw output across identical calls | |
fix: The test was asserting something that is not unconditionally true, so it now asserts three separate things that are, rather than being quietly relaxed until it passed: 1. Decision-relevant fields are stable even from cold — code and confidence never moved. This is the claim that matters, since no policy rule reads the prose. 2. Raw output is byte-identical once resident, with an explicit warm-up call. That is the real operating condition: keep_alive is 30 minutes and a batch is hundreds of sequential calls. 3. num_ctx is a pure function of the prompt, so it cannot drift between runs. The important part: none of this threatens reproducibility, because reproducibility here never rested on the model. It rests on the committed cache. A call is made once, its exact bytes are stored in .llm_cache/, and every later run — including --offline on a machine with no model installed — replays those bytes. Model determinism is a bonus; cache determinism is the guarantee, and it is absolute. Discovering this made the project's actual reproducibility argument clearer rather than weaker.

title: the prompt was 90% of the cost, in the wrong order
symptom: The 40-record benchmark was crawling: 5 calls in 20 minutes, roughly 4 minutes per call, against a doctor estimate of about 33 seconds.
wrong_hypothesis: "Two workers are oversubscribing the CPU." Plausible — the batch runner's own docstring warns about exactly that — but measuring it showed 2 workers were *faster* than 1 (22.9 vs 29.6 s/call). Parallelism was not the problem.
cause: Reading the timings straight out of the cache entries: | | tokens | time | |
fix: Two changes to classify/prompts.py: 1. Invert the order. Static preamble (codes, rules, output contract) first; case data last. ~491 tokens of identical prefix now sit at the front of every prompt in the batch, leaving ~190 tokens of genuinely new work per call. 2. Say each thing once. The reason-code list carried a prose label for every code when the codes are already self-describing. Glosses kept only where the name is ambiguous. Measured: 48.5 → 22.9 s/call, a 2.1x speedup. The token count fell only 23% (1084 → 837 including the system prompt), so most of the gain is the prefix cache, not the trim. doctor was also rebuilt to probe with a *realistic* prompt — its old 20-token ping measured generation speed and ignored the 90% of the work that is prompt evaluation, and happened to produce a roughly-right total only by cancelling two errors. Worth keeping: on local inference, measure where the time actually goes before optimising the thing the documentation says is expensive. And treat prompt *order* as a performance decision, not just a readability one.

title: the benchmark measured an impossible task
symptom: First real benchmark: macro-F1 0.431 against a 0.72 floor, with 0% abstention. The model was confidently wrong rather than uncertain.
wrong_hypothesis: "A 7B is too small for a 19-class taxonomy; escalate to the 12B." That would have cost a 9 GB download and several hours, and it would not have helped.
cause: The confusion matrix pointed straight at it — six of the errors were TDS_194C/H/J → TDS_RATE_MISMATCH, all in the same direction: valid statutory withholding being flagged as a chaseable error. That is the single most expensive mistake this system can make, so it was worth checking whether the model was wrong or the *label* was. The label was. Measuring the generated data: - 75 of 107 valid plain-TDS deductions sat under a section the contract did not expect. - 15 of 15 TDS_RATE_MISMATCH cases had an implied rate that is itself a real statutory rate. The generator drew the TDS section from the mix *independently of the contract*. So a 10% deduction against a 194C-at-2% contract was labelled "valid TDS_194J" in some rows and "invalid TDS_RATE_MISMATCH" in others, with byte-identical observable data. The label was not identifiable from anything the agent can see. No classifier can beat chance on that subset, and 0.431 was a measurement of a data bug rather than of the model.
fix: A legitimate withholding now uses the section *and* rate pinned on the contract (Contract.tds_rate_expected_bp, added in the same pass for the same reason). A drawn section that does not match is substituted, not rejected — rejecting it sent the draw back to the mix and collapsed the TDS-family share from ~38% to 23%, which quietly guts the batch's central premise, since the statutory "do not chase" majority is precisely what a naive agent fails on. After: 0 unidentifiable valid-TDS cases, 0 unidentifiable rate-mismatch cases, TDS share back to 42.5%, and oracle verification still exactly 100%. Worth keeping: when a model underperforms, read the confusion matrix before reaching for a bigger model. A systematic error in one direction is far more often a broken label than a weak classifier — and here the "obvious" fix would have burned an afternoon and left the real bug in place, silently capping the headline accuracy of the whole project.

title: a helpful hint that made the model worse
symptom: Added a deterministic feasibility layer — compute which codes are physically possible for each case, list them in the prompt, and treat an impossible answer as an abstention. It should have helped on every axis. Measured: macro-F1 fell from 0.554 to 0.512 and latency rose from 61.3s to 69.9s per call.
wrong_hypothesis: "Noise on n=40." A two-case difference plausibly is. But the confusion matrix was not noise-shaped at all — it had collapsed onto two codes: Eleven wrong answers of UNEARNED_DISCOUNT and six of TDS_RATE_MISMATCH, on cases that were nothing of the sort.
cause: Those are precisely the two codes my new hints *named*: > "contract offers NO early-payment discount, so any discount the buyer took is > unearned by definition" > "deduction rate EXCEEDS the contracted TDS rate — if this is TDS, it is > TDS_RATE_MISMATCH" Both were written as conditionals and both were meant to be disqualifying context. A 7B model does not carry the conditional. It carries the label. Mentioning a code — in any framing, however carefully hedged — makes the model reach for it, and since most contracts have no discount clause, that first hint was firing on most of the batch as a standing suggestion to answer UNEARNED_DISCOUNT.
fix: A hard rule, now enforced by test_hints_never_name_a_reason_code: computed hints state facts only and never name a reason code. "contract contains no early-payment discount clause" rather than "...so any discount is unearned". The decision rules in the static preamble do the mapping from fact to code; the per-case block supplies only evidence. Worth keeping: this is the counterintuitive one. Extra context that reads as obviously helpful to a human can be actively harmful to a small model, because a mentioned label is an available label. And it would have been easy to accept 0.512 as noise, ship it, and carry an invisible bias into every number downstream — the confusion matrix is what distinguished "slightly unlucky" from "systematically steered". The post-hoc feasibility *gate* was kept regardless of its effect on F1: it is free, it is deterministic, and it is the project's only real abstention signal. The model's self-reported confidence was measured at 0.95 on 34 of 40 cases — identical for easy and hard ones — so a confidence threshold would never fire and would give a false sense of safety. "This answer is physically impossible for this case" is evidence; "I am 95% sure" is not.

title: a 100% match rate against mostly-wrong allocations
symptom: First run of the matching stage: 218 of 218 payments matched, 100%. It looked finished.
cause: The reconciliation check — does the shortfall derived from allocations agree with what was actually deducted? — said 60 invoices disagreed, and only 83 of 400 invoices had any allocation at all. A 100% match rate over 83 invoices is not a match rate, it is 218 payments piled onto the same small set. The cause: I picked the *first* remittance advice for each buyer and reused it for every one of that buyer's payments. Four separate bugs came out of pulling that thread, and each was invisible to the match rate: 1. Advice reuse. Fixed by consuming advices one-to-one. 2. Date-proximity linking. Pairing an advice to the nearest payment attached an advice naming INV-0062 to the credit that settled INV-0003 — then reported it as a high-confidence "the advice named this invoice" match. Fixed by linking on amount: an advice's net lines must sum to the credit it describes. Date is only a tie-breaker. 3. Fuzzy matching on short strings. INV/2026/0003 generates the variant 20263, and the bare year token 2026 scores 88.9 against it — over an 88 threshold. Six payments belonging to other invoices were allocated to INV-0003 on that basis. Fixed by excluding bare years and requiring six characters for fuzzy comparison. 4. Truncated references matching exactly. INV20260+3MORE is a seven-invoice bundle whose reference list did not fit; the surviving fragment happened to equal a short invoice's variant, and matching on it posted a ₹54,89,008 bundle against a ₹1,45,316 invoice. I was already detecting truncation — but only to write a nicer error message. Fixed by discarding truncated tokens before matching, not after. Two more followed: 5. Sequential allocation on bundles. Filling invoices largest-first puts the entire shortfall on whichever invoice comes last, inventing a large deduction on one and none on the others — and it reconciles perfectly at the payment level. Fixed by using the advice's per-invoice net figures. 6. Double allocation. A bundle and a later subset-sum match both claimed INV-0000, allocating ₹60,562 against a ₹36,394 invoice. That shows as a *zero delta*, silently erasing a real deduction. Fixed with a cumulative per-invoice cap.
result: Match rate fell to 83.5% and money located rose to 77.9% of the true deduction total, with 36 payments declined into the exceptions report. The rate went down and the system got better. Worth keeping: a match rate is not a measure of matching. It rewards exactly the behaviour it should punish — a matcher that guesses beats one that abstains on every metric except the one that matters. The reconciliation check found all six of these; the match rate found none of them, and looked healthy throughout.

title: the agent scored perfectly by doing nothing
symptom: First end-to-end run: 308 cases, all closed as resolved_closed_valid, zero contacts sent, zero false chases. A flawless harm score and 100% auto-resolution.
wrong_hypothesis: Briefly, that the policy engine was being appropriately conservative.
cause: Only ~50 of 308 deductions had been classified at that point. The rest had verdict='unknown' and recoverable_paise=0 — not because they were legitimate, but because nobody had looked at them. And the stopping rule read: recoverable_paise <= 0 is true for a verified-valid deduction *and* for one that was never examined. The agent was recording "correctly did not chase" for 258 cases it had never looked at. This is the most flattering possible bug: it produces a perfect harm number, a perfect auto-resolution rate, and zero cost, by doing no work at all. Every headline metric moves the right way.
fix: The rule now requires an actual adjudication — verdict in {valid, provisional_valid} — and an unknown verdict routes to the human queue under a separate named rule, stopping.not_verified. "We never looked" and "we checked and it was fine" are different outcomes and now say so in the decision log. Worth keeping: be most suspicious of the result you wanted. A metric that improves because a stage silently did nothing looks identical to one that improves because the stage worked.

title: the draft validator rejected every valid message
symptom: test_static_templates_all_pass_their_own_validator failed on all seven templates with unverified_amount:125.
cause: The validator normalises rupee figures before comparing them, and stripped trailing zeros to make 12500.00 compare equal to 12500. Applied unconditionally, that turns the *integer* 12500 into 125. So every correctly-drafted message mentioning a round amount — which is most of them — was rejected as containing an invented figure. Every draft would have fallen back to the template, and the validator-rejection metric would have read 100% while looking exactly like the control working as designed.
fix: Strip trailing zeros only after a decimal point. Worth keeping: the test that caught this validates the *static templates* against their own validator — components that both sit on the happy path and would otherwise never be checked against each other. It was written to catch a template edited to include a forbidden phrase; it caught a bug in the validator instead.

title: the same batch matched differently in every process
symptom: "Money located by matching" would not hold still. Successive measurements of the *same* batch gave 77.6%, then 98.4% three times in a row, then 77.9% — with an identical database content hash (9546896f…) and no code changes between them. Wrong hypotheses, in order. Three, and each one cost time: 1. *"A previous run persisted state that feeds back in."* Checked: zero allocations, zero recovery payments, nothing classified. Ruled out. 2. *"The background classification job is mutating the database underneath the measurement."* Genuinely true and worth fixing — generate was silently failing with PermissionError because another process held the SQLite file, and fixtures are written *before* the database reset, so it left a torn state. But stopping that job did not make the number stable. 3. *"I corrected the figure wrongly earlier."* I did in fact publish 98.2%, correct it to 77.6%, then un-correct it back to 98.4% — each time on the evidence in front of me, each time reproducible *within* the session. The correction churn was a symptom, not carelessness.
cause: fuzzy_variants was built by iterating a set: Python randomises string hashing per process, so that list is in a different order every time the interpreter starts. When two variants tie on fuzzy score, rapidfuzz.extractOne returns whichever it saw first — so the same payment matched to a different invoice depending on the process, and roughly 20 percentage points of "money located" rode on it. Every individual run was internally consistent. Measuring three times in one process gave the same answer three times, which reads as proof of determinism and is not — it is proof that one interpreter's hash seed is stable. The existing determinism test had exactly this shape and passed throughout. The replacement test runs matching in two separate subprocesses and compares the allocations. It fails on the old code and passes on the new. Worth keeping: two things. Determinism tests must cross a process boundary, or they only assert that a hash seed is stable within one run. And when a number will not hold still, suspect the measurement apparatus before re-deriving the number — I published three different figures for this before finding the one-word cause, and each correction was made in good faith on reproducible-looking evidence.

title: the counterparty never paid anybody
symptom: First real scoreboard. Every policy recovered exactly ₹0 — including B1, which had sent 677 chase letters.
wrong_hypothesis: "The agent is conservative because most deductions are still unclassified." True for the *agent*, and it made the zero look explicable. It does not explain B1, which chases regardless of classification and should have collected from every buyer whose ground truth says they pay when chased.
cause: state.cases was keyed by deduction id (DED-0000-0) while _deliver_inbound looked cases up by case id (CASE-0000-0): So no inbound event was ever applied. No payments, no disputes, no promises, no opt-outs. The counterparty state machine ran, scheduled events correctly, and had every one of them silently dropped on delivery.
fix: Key the dict by case id. After: B1 recovers ₹6,17,849 from 669 contacts, with 473 false chases — which is the harm contrast the whole project is built to show. Worth keeping: the signal was a *baseline behaving implausibly*, not the agent. A system where the agent recovers nothing is ambiguous — it might be being careful. A system where blanket dunning sends 677 letters and collects nothing is not ambiguous; no real dunning process is that bad. The new test asserts on B1 rather than the agent for exactly that reason: the agent legitimately recovers nothing when its inputs are unclassified, so it cannot carry this check. Two smaller faults surfaced in the same pass: recovery payments were keyed by case rather than by inbound event, so a second credit scheduled before the first landed collided on the primary key; and run_batch relied on the CLI to clear prior state, so any direct call collided on Case ids. It now clears its own state and is idempotent.

title: the agent's own recoveries polluted the matcher
symptom: Immediately after the feedback loop started working, the matching test failed: match rate had dropped from 83.5% to 77.1%. Nothing in the matcher had changed.
cause: The tick loop writes a PaymentEvent for every recovered credit, so the agent's successes are persisted as bank credits. The next run_matching picked them up and tried to allocate them against invoices — but they correspond to no invoice, so they landed in the exceptions report and dragged the denominator down. The matcher was being asked to reconcile money the agent had generated itself.
fix: Matching now reads only genuine bank-statement credits (recovery_for_case_id is None). Worth keeping: a stage that writes into a table an earlier stage reads from has created a feedback loop, whether or not anyone intended one. This was caught by a test on a completely different phase, which is the argument for keeping phase-level acceptance tests green continuously rather than at the end.

title: four cases collected exactly twice
symptom: Building the summary PDF, the funnel chart showed "Addressed" (Rs 23,27,694) sitting above the "reachable ceiling" (Rs 22,49,826). That is arithmetically impossible: recovered money and escalated money are disjoint subsets of what is reachable, so their sum cannot exceed it.
cause: A case can be contacted twice before the first payment lands — contact on day 1 schedules a credit for day 5, contact on day 4 schedules another for day 8. _deliver_inbound applied both, accumulating recovered_paise twice. Four cases collected exactly double their true recoverable amount. The headline numbers moved by a lot: agent recovery Rs 4,10,864 -> Rs 2,61,722, B1 Rs 6,17,849 -> Rs 5,15,167. Every policy had been over-reporting, which is why the comparison still looked sane.
fix: A settled case stays settled — a PAYMENT event arriving at a case already in RESOLVED_RECOVERED is marked delivered and ignored. Verified across all five policies: zero cases now recover more than ground truth allows, and addressed <= ceiling holds everywhere. Worth keeping: the only reason this surfaced is that a chart put two numbers next to each other that had a *required* relationship. Rs 4.1L of recovery is entirely plausible on its own and would have shipped unquestioned. Invariants between figures catch what individually-plausible figures never will — and a diagram is a surprisingly good place to discover one, because it forces quantities into the same frame.

title: the site rendered as a black screen, and the first diagnosis was wrong
symptom: The React front end replaced the Streamlit dashboard. The hero rendered perfectly. Everything below it — six sections, about 15,000px of content — was pure black. The DOM was intact: main.innerText.length was 47,614, elementFromPoint returned real paragraphs at the coordinates that looked empty, and every element reported opacity: 1, visibility: visible, correct bounding boxes and the right colours. Separately, only 2 of 34 scroll-reveal elements had ever been marked visible.
wrong_hypothesis: Confidently. A fixed, full-viewport overlay carried mix-blend-mode: overlay. A blend mode composites against its stacking context's backdrop, so a fixed full-viewport blend layer promotes the entire document to one composited layer — and this document is very tall. The story wrote itself: Chrome gives up on the layer, stops painting below the fold, stops delivering IntersectionObserver callbacks, every .reveal stays at opacity: 0. It explained all three symptoms at once. It was wrong. Removing the blend mode changed nothing — reveals went from 2 to 5 to 3 across attempts, which read as "partially fixed" and kept the theory alive for another twenty minutes.
cause: The browser pane was hidden. Counting animation-frame callbacks over one second settled it — the loop below never completed: requestAnimationFrame was not firing at all, while document.visibilityState still reported "visible" and setTimeout worked normally. No frames means no rendering steps, which means no IntersectionObserver callbacks and no compositor output for a screenshot. The page was correct the entire time; the harness looking at it was not producing frames. The blend mode was innocent. It was removed anyway — a full-page blend layer over 15,000px is a real cost for a grain texture that a plain low-opacity overlay reproduces — but the comment in web/src/index.css no longer claims it fixed anything, because it did not.
fix: The genuine defect was upstream of both theories: the design hid its own content by default. .reveal starts at opacity: 0 and waits for a callback that is not guaranteed to arrive. Anything that starves the frame loop — an occluded window, a throttled background tab, an overloaded compositor — turns the whole site black, and that failure is indistinguishable from a data-loading bug. The first fix was wrong too, and worth recording. It probed the frame loop once on mount: request a frame, race it against a 1.2s timeout, and if no frame arrived reveal everything. That covers "frames never start". It does not cover "frames start and then stop", which is the actual case — the probe settles *alive* during load and disarms itself, and the window is occluded a second later. Measured afterwards: 0 frames in 600 ms with all 37 reveals still hidden. What ships instead has no frame dependency at all. IntersectionObserver remains the fast path, and a single shared, passive scroll listener re-checks anything still hidden with getBoundingClientRect. Scroll events are input-driven rather than frame-driven, so they arrive when frames do not. The check asks "has the reader reached it", not "is it on screen right now" — the listener is debounced, so a fast scroll lands between samples and an intersection test would strand whatever flew past. That last change exposed a third bug hiding under the first two. The observer callback was setInView(e.isIntersecting), which writes false for anything off screen — including elements the fallback had already revealed and dropped from its pending set. Ten of thirty-seven ended up hidden, scrolled past, and watched by neither mechanism. Under once, the observer now only ever sets true. Worth keeping: two things. Determinism tests must cross a process boundary, or they only assert that a hash seed is stable within one run. And when a number will not hold still, suspect the measurement apparatus before re-deriving the number — I published three different figures for this before finding the one-word cause, and each correction was made in good faith on reproducible-looking evidence.
